topic: Note 1: consolidation policy
claim: Note 1 said Enron's consolidated statements included 'all subsidiaries controlled by Enron Corp.' It did not explain the special rules under which Enron kept SPEs and partnerships it effectively sponsored out of its statements.
quote: The consolidated financial statements include the accounts of all subsidiaries controlled by Enron Corp. after the elimination of significant intercompany accounts and transactions.

locator.section: Note 1 Summary of Significant Accounting Policies - Consolidation Policy and Use of Estimates

notes: The policy statement is standard. The problem was in applying it: on Nov 8, 2001 Enron itself concluded that Chewco, JEDI and an LJM1 subsidiary should have been consolidated (see N-032 and A-085). The same note warns that 'Actual results could differ from those estimates' (line 4107), a routine sentence that matters more for a company using mark-to-market. Related existing cards: A-030, A-085, A-083.
checker_note: Fingerprint OK. Quote verbatim at 10-K lines 4096-4099. Claim OK: a text search of the whole 10-K finds no mention of special purpose entities or non-consolidation rules. (Phase 2 Fact-Checker A, 2026-09-27)

topic: Note 1: estimates

locator.section: Note 1 - Consolidation Policy and Use of Estimates

notes: Boilerplate found in almost every 10-K; useful for teaching because Enron's mark-to-market values were largely estimates (see Note 1 price risk management policy, A-020). Related existing cards: A-020.

topic: Note 1: mark-to-market policy (reuse)
claim: Note 1's 'Accounting for Price Risk Management' paragraph is the heart of mark-to-market: trading contracts at fair value, unrealized gains (including on newly signed contracts) recorded as revenue, prices based on 'management's best estimate.'
quote: Instruments utilized in connection with trading activities are accounted for using the mark-to-market method.

locator.section: Note 1 - Accounting for Price Risk Management

notes: Pointer card: the full analysis is in A-020 (do not duplicate). Later view: the Senate PSI staff found the board was told in 1999 about expanding fair value accounting and in May 2000 did not object to 'the more aggressive valuation model' (N-009). Related existing cards: A-020, A-022, A-023.
checker_note: Fingerprint OK. Quote verbatim at lines 4155-4156; 'management's best estimate' at line 4172. Pointer card; claim OK. (Phase 2 Fact-Checker A, 2026-09-27)

topic: Note 1: unconsolidated affiliates and merchant investments
claim: Note 1 said investments in unconsolidated affiliates used the equity method, except merchant investments carried at market value, pointing readers to Notes 4 and 9.
quote: Investments in unconsolidated affiliates are accounted for by the equity method, except for certain investments resulting from Enron's merchant investment activities which are included at market value in "Other Investments" in the Consolidated Balance Sheet.
notes: Plain language: 'equity method' = Enron records its share of the affiliate's profit or loss as one line, without putting the affiliate's debts on Enron's balance sheet. This is the bridge from Note 1 to Notes 4 and 9.
checker_note: Fingerprint OK. Quote verbatim at lines 4233-4237 (the note continues 'See Notes 4 and 9'). Claim OK. (Phase 2 Fact-Checker A, 2026-09-27)

topic: Note 3: 'notional amounts' caveat

topic: Note 3: securitizations and Whitewing
claim: Note 3 disclosed that in 2000 Enron recognized $381 million of gains on 'securitizations' (sales of interests in financial assets), with $2,379 million of proceeds, $545 million of which came from sales to Whitewing Associates.

notes: Whitewing was a 50%-owned Enron affiliate (Note 9). The bankruptcy examiner later concluded that Enron's 'FAS 140 Transactions' (its securitizations) were 'essentially bridge financings of illiquid assets' in which Enron kept the risk (A-067, A-068). The note also says Enron 'concurrently enters into swaps ... which limits the risks assumed by the purchaser' (lines 4458-4460): a hint that risk stayed with Enron. Related existing cards: A-067, A-068, A-074.

topic: Note 3: credit risk and collateral
claim: Note 3 said Enron held 'credit and other reserves' of $452 million against its trading assets, that about $16.7 billion of $21.5 billion was with investment-grade counterparties, and that Enron held about $5.5 billion of collateral, mostly customer cash deposits.
quote: At December 31, 2000, Enron held collateral of approximately $5.5 billion, which consists substantially of cash deposits shown as "Customers' Deposits" on the balance sheet.
notes: The reverse also applied: Enron had to post collateral to its counterparties if its own rating fell. The Q3 2001 10-Q warned that a downgrade 'could lead to a substantial increase in the level of cash required for collateral' (A-079). Note 3 describes others' credit risk to Enron, not Enron's own. Related existing cards: A-079.

locator.section: Finding (2) High Risk Accounting - Other Evidence of Board Awareness

Cite PSI, not the 8-K; if a figure is used, say 'up to $10 billion' or give both.

notes: The Senate Governmental Affairs staff (N-028) called the omitted magnitude 'a whopping $4 billion.' The Q3 10-Q put potential repayments at $3.9 billion (A-080) and gave Osprey/Marlin trigger prices of $59.78 and $34.13 with the stock at $9.00 on Nov 16, 2001 (N-025). Related existing cards: A-080.
checker_note: Fingerprint OK. Quote verbatim at lines 2950-2953. Claim OK. The $4B vs $3.9B disagreement is noted. (Phase 2 Fact-Checker A, 2026-09-27)

topic: Later view: SEC did not review the 2000 10-K (Senate Governmental Affairs)
claim: The Senate Governmental Affairs Committee staff reported that the SEC reviewed Enron's 10-Ks for 1991, 1995, 1996 and 1997, but none of the 10-Ks for 1998, 1999 or 2000.

topic: Later view: other red flags in the 2000 10-K (Senate Governmental Affairs)
claim: Besides Note 16, the Senate staff listed items in the 2000 10-K that might have prompted questions: Note 9's 50%-owned affiliates, the MD&A's stock-price early-settlement contracts (with no size given, later shown to be about $4 billion), and the 'refined' value-at-risk model.

claim: The Senate PSI staff found the 1999 and 2000 related-party footnotes, about one page each, 'nearly unintelligible,' while the November 19, 2001 10-Q gave a nine-page, much clearer account, showing Enron 'was quite capable of meaningful public disclosure when motivated.'

topic: Later view: disclosure failure summarized (Powers)
claim: The Powers Committee found that Enron disclosed that there were large transactions with entities in which the CFO had an interest, but never clearly disclosed their purposes, the CFO's benefits, or their full financial-statement effects, and that responsibility was shared by management, the Audit Committee, in-house counsel, Vinson & Elkins and Andersen.
quote: Overall, Enron failed to disclose facts that were important for an understanding of the substance of the transactions.
notes: Process (pp. 181-182): footnote drafts were prepared by the Financial Reporting Group, but accountants and lawyers 'generally deferred to' Fastow's Enron Global Finance group; Causey was 'the final arbiter'; all directors and Fastow signed the 10-K. fn-01 already cites p. 178 for Note 16; this card is the general statement. Related existing cards: A-064, fn-01.

topic: Later view: substance over technical correctness (Batson)
claim: The bankruptcy examiner concluded that Enron's reporting was materially misleading because it failed to disclose the substance of the transactions, whether or not the accounting was technically correct.
quote: Enron's financial reporting of the transactions discussed in the Reports resulted in the materially misleading presentation of Enron's financial condition by failing to disclose the substance of such transactions, regardless of whether the accounting was technically correct.
notes: Verified on page image PDF p. 24 (same page as A-070). The pathway's closing lesson: a note can be accurate line by line and still hide the story. Related existing cards: A-070.

topic: Nov 8, 2001 8-K: what Enron said the notes had missed
claim: In its November 8, 2001 8-K, Enron said three unconsolidated entities should have been consolidated, based on 'information made available from further review of certain related-party transactions,' and that its 1997-2000 statements and audit reports should not be relied upon. It explained that consolidating Chewco/JEDI added their debt and removed JEDI revenues from appreciation of Enron stock.
quote: Enron's net income is reduced for specific JEDI revenues previously allocated to Chewco, relating to the appreciation in value of Enron stock, which eliminate upon consolidation.
